title: An imprint method to produce surface asperities for EHL and RCF experiments
author: Everitt, Alfredsson, et al.

steps.title: Manufacture blank discs
steps.instruction: Produce three blank disc blanks that will become the indent‑disc, the asperity‑disc, and the counter‑disc.

steps.title: Harden indent disc
steps.instruction: Heat‑treat the blank designated as the indent‑disc to achieve the required hardness for subsequent imprinting.

steps.title: Create Rockwell cone indents
steps.instruction: Using a Rockwell cone indenter, generate the desired indents on the hardened indent‑disc.

steps.title: Remove pile‑up around indents
steps.instruction: Machining or polishing steps are applied to eliminate the pile‑up material that forms around each indent on the indent‑disc.

steps.title: Imprint asperities via rolling
steps.instruction: Roll the soft blank disc (to become the asperity‑disc) against the hardened indent‑disc so that the indent pattern is transferred as integrated asperities of 4–15 µm height and 100–200 µm diameter.

steps.title: Harden asperity and counter discs
steps.instruction: Heat‑treat both the newly imprinted asperity‑disc and the separate counter‑disc to the required hardness for the EHL and RCF tests.

steps.title: Conduct EHL experiments
steps.instruction: Assemble the hardened asperity‑disc and counter‑disc in the elastohydrodynamic lubrication test rig and run the EHL experiments.

description: A method was developed for manufacturing single asperities integrated into the hard contact surfaces of rolling contact discs for use in experimental investigations of the influence of single asperities on rolling contact fatigue (RCF) in hard lubricated and rolling contacts. The method is important for the experimental verification of the asperity point load mechanism for RCF [1], [2], [3], [4], [5] which suggests a plausible model for the initiation of surface initiated RCF. A series of experimental RCF set-ups exist [6], ranging from product tests of bearings and gears, to surface experiments in twin-disc testers. Some experiments focus on the influence of dents [7] or grooves [8] on RCF and lubrication film properties. The reversed surface design, with individual ridges or asperities is harder to manufacture. Local material deposit is one method. It works for lubrication studies with limited cycle numbers and contact pressures. The challenge remains to deposit material that endure millions of over-rolling cycles at extreme RCF pressures. Indentations have been used to create point defects by numerous researchers. For instance Ville and Nelias [9], Coulin et al. [10], Lorösch [11] and Dommarco et al. [12] have investigated effects of indents on RCF. The experiments show that indents reduce the fatigue lives of the surfaces by creating pressure peaks. The indents are often connected with a circumventing pile-up ring. Following the asperity point load mechanism, RCF cracks initiate at the trailing edge of the pile-up and grow in the forward rolling direction at a shallow angle. However, these undulation become 5 to 100 times larger than asperities in applications; it contains a deep dent which serves as an oil reservoir; the material structure is heavily deformed, which affects fatigue properties and residual stresses; it can be hard to separate the effects of the pile-up from those of the indent on RCF life.
